text: Downtown Calgary is in the wrong place.
The towers, the main street, the railway line: none of it stands where the town began.
Calgary started on one side of a river.
Then a railway company moved it to the other.
This is how that happened.
Start at the water.
Here, the Elbow River bends north and runs into the Bow.
The Blackfoot call this place Mo-kin-stiss, the elbow.
People met, traded and crossed the rivers here long before anyone drew a map of it.
In eighteen seventy-five a troop of the North West Mounted Police rode up from the south.
Their job was to shut down the illegal whisky trade.
They built a wooden post on the point of land where the rivers meet.
Its commander, a young inspector named Ephrem Breez-bwah, named the fort after himself.
He had no authority to do that, and his superiors cancelled the order.
In eighteen seventy-six the post got a new name, borrowed from a place on the Isle of Mull in Scotland.
Fort Calgary.
A year later, in eighteen seventy-seven, Treaty Seven was signed at Blackfoot Crossing, down the Bow.
Around the fort, a settlement took shape.
Traders, a few log buildings, and rows of tents.
Most of it stood on the east bank of the Elbow, where the neighbourhood of Inglewood is today.
Then came the news everyone on the prairies was waiting for.
The Canadian Pacific Railway was building west, and it was coming straight through.
A railway station made a town. Everybody knew it.
So people bought land on the east bank, as close to the settlement as they could get.
Lots were selling fast. The main street was already picked out.
In the summer of eighteen eighty-three the track layers reached the Bow.
And the people of Calgary were about to find out that the railway had a different plan.
In August eighteen eighty-three a railway company looked at a brand-new town, and built its station somewhere else.
To see why, look at the land the way a surveyor did.
The prairie was cut into square sections, each one a mile across, each with a number.
The settlement sat on Section Fourteen, east of the Elbow.
Next door to the west was Section Fifteen.
Section Fifteen was nearly empty. The Mounted Police used it to graze their horses.
It also had one feature that mattered more than any building.
The railway had been granted odd-numbered sections along its line.
On Section Fourteen, the land was already in other hands.
Section Fifteen could belong to the company.
The railway secured Section Fifteen through an order from the federal cabinet.
On the fifteenth of August eighteen eighty-three the bridge over the Elbow was finished.
The first train rolled across the river, past the settlement, and stopped about a mile to the west.
That spot is where Palliser Square stands today, beside the Calgary Tower.
There was no grand station.
Calgary's first one was the body of a boxcar, set down beside the track.
The reason for the choice is not hard to read, though this part is interpretation.
On Section Fourteen, speculators would have made the money.
On Section Fifteen, every lot belonged to the railway.
And the railway started selling.
A corner lot cost four hundred and fifty dollars.
Buyers who built before April got half their money back.
So many people wanted in that names were drawn from a hat.
The first name out was John Glenn, one of the earliest settlers in the area.
More than a hundred lots sold on the first day.
Still, a town is more than lots on a plan.
The shops, the homes and the people were on the far side of the river.
To pull them across, the railway needed one small building.
The post office.
One winter morning, the story goes, Calgary woke up and its post office was gone.
In eighteen eighty-three a post office was the reason to come into town.
Whoever had it, had the traffic.
Calgary's was run by James Bannerman, who also kept a flour and feed store on the east bank.
People asked the government to move it closer to the station. The government was slow.
So the railway made its own offer: one hundred dollars in cash, and two free lots in the new townsite.
What happened next is told a few different ways.
In the best-known version, the railway's engineer, Herbert Holt, hitched a team to the building and hauled it across the frozen Elbow.
The details change with the teller. The result does not.
The post office ended up on the west side.
After that, the town let go.
That winter, owners moved their buildings across the ice.
In the spring of eighteen eighty-four a billiard hall made the same trip and reopened on the new main street, Stephen Avenue.
Not everyone was happy.
In January eighteen eighty-four a notice went round calling a public meeting.
About four hundred people now lived here, and they wanted two things:
a bridge over the Elbow, and a committee to speak for them.
They got both. A wooden bridge went up beside the railway's own.
On the seventh of November eighteen eighty-four, Calgary became a town, the first in what is now Alberta.
It had five hundred and six people, and a harness maker named George Murdoch as its first mayor.
The grid the railway's surveyor drew became the downtown streets.
The old settlement on the east bank became the quiet edge of town.
The move was complete.
The new Calgary was built fast, close together, and mostly of wood.
Two years later, to the day, it caught fire.
On the seventh of November eighteen eighty-six, Calgary had two things to celebrate.
By the end of the day, part of its main street was ash.
It was the town's second birthday.
It was also one year since the last spike finished the railway to the Pacific.
Early that Sunday morning, flames were seen at the back wall of a flour and feed store.
The buildings around it were wood, and the fire moved from one to the next.
Calgary did have a fire engine.
The town council had ordered it, and it had arrived.
But nobody had the authority to pay for it, so it sat in a railway freight shed.
That morning a group of men broke it out.
To slow the fire, they pulled down buildings in its path, among them George Murdoch's harness shop.
Nobody was killed. Nobody was hurt.
About eighteen buildings were gone.
What the town did next changed how it looked for a generation.
Under the land around Calgary lies a pale, tough rock called Paska-poo sandstone.
Over the following years more than a dozen quarries opened inside what are now the city limits.
Banks, churches and, in nineteen eleven, City Hall rose in stone.
Calgary earned a nickname: the Sandstone City.
There is a catch in the tidy version.
Calgary was not all wood before the fire.
Two sandstone buildings were already standing on Eighth Avenue that morning.
The fire did not start the idea. It made the argument impossible to ignore.
In eighteen ninety-four Calgary became a city, with thirty-nine hundred people.
Today more than one point three million live here.
The old townsite is Inglewood.
The spot where a boxcar once served as a station sits beside the Calgary Tower.
A railway's land deal decided where this city would stand.
So here is the question.
Who is deciding the shape of Calgary today, and do you have a say?
